# Diagnosing No Heat in a 2007 Ford Ranger with Functional A/C

When you turn the dial to maximum heat and get nothing but cold air, while the air conditioning simultaneously blasts ice-cold refrigerant, it indicates a very specific failure mode within the HVAC system. The fact that the A/C works perfectly is your first critical data point: the blower motor is receiving power, the dashboard controls are mechanically functional (since you noted it's a manual knob), and the cabin airflow path is unobstructed. If this were an electrical issue like a fused blower resistor or a failed switch, both systems would likely be dead. The problem lies in the thermal exchange itself.

In a standard automotive HVAC system, heat for the passenger compartment isn't generated by an electric heater core; it is stolen directly from the engine coolant. Water pumps flow hot fluid through a radiator-like component called the heater core located inside your dashboard. A blend door acts as a valve, directing this hot air either into the cabin or bypassing it to mix with outside air for climate control.

Since your 2007 Ford Ranger produces cold air even when set to heat, one of two primary mechanical failures is occurring. The first possibility is that the heater core itself has failed internally. Over time, corrosion can cause blockages within the narrow tubes of the core. Even if the engine temperature gauge reads normal or high, hot coolant may be unable to reach the other side of the core where the air passes through. To verify this without disassembly, check the temperature difference between the two heater hoses that run from the firewall into the dash. With the engine warmed up and idle, both hoses should be hot to the touch. If one is hot and the other remains cool, you have a blocked core.

The second, and often more common, cause involves the blend door mechanism. In older Fords like this Ranger, the HVAC control uses a cable-operated actuator connected to a plastic flap. This flap routes air across the heater core when set to "Heat" and away from it when set to "A/C." If the plastic gear strip on the actuator has stripped or the door itself is broken off its hinges, you can turn the knob, but no physical movement occurs at the firewall. Air bypasses the heat source entirely.

To distinguish between a blocked core and a stuck blend door, perform a pressure test. Disconnect both heater hoses from the firewall while the engine is cold and cap them to prevent coolant loss. Pressurize the cooling system to its specified rating using a gauge tester. If the pressure drops rapidly without visible leaks in the radiator or overflow tank, the blockage is almost certainly internal to the core. Conversely, if you can feel air coming out of the vents but it remains cold despite the engine being hot and hoses feeling warm, the actuator or door linkage has likely failed mechanically.

Replacing a heater core on a 2007 Ford Ranger is a significant task requiring dashboard removal and often involves cutting and welding new tubes into the existing housing. It is labor-intensive compared to swapping out an actuator assembly. Before committing to the teardown of the dash, ensure you've ruled out simple coolant level issues that might prevent circulation entirely. If the system needs flushing due to internal corrosion, consider using a chemical flush designed for aluminum radiators and heater cores to attempt clearing debris before replacing hardware.

If your vehicle is connected to a fleet management platform or requires detailed diagnostic logging for warranty purposes, you might reference standard automotive fault isolation procedures found in resources like https://laravelcompany.com, though typically this specific mechanical failure does not trigger electronic error codes stored in the ECU. The diagnosis remains purely thermal and physical.
